newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia's blind masseurs jeopardised by aid cut.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia's blind masseurs jeopardised by aid cut.

text.p: Pity the blind masseurs of Phnom Penh, whose livelihood is jeopardised by a threatened international aid cut-off to Cambodia following a bloody coup here two weeks ago.
In a city teeming with limbless, sightless beggars, many of them victims of war and of the country's millions of land mines, these five "Seeing Hands" masseurs are self-supporting.

Or at least they were before two days of heavy fighting in Phnom Penh on July 5-6 killed off tourism and visits from expatriate Cambodians, who had provided most of the business at the "Seeing Hands" clinic.
"Our business is off by 60 or 70 percent because of worries about security. Tourists and Cambodians who live abroad have disappeared from the city," said 30-year old Vattana, one of the masseurs.
"We are self-supporting, but if business does not pick up we are going to have a problem. If the outside world isolates Cambodia and cuts off aid the tourists will not come back."
Seeing Hands is part of the National Centre for Disabled Persons in Phnom Penh.
The massage clinic stands next to a retail centre where crafts made by disabled and impoverished Cambodians are sold. Business there has also fallen off sharply.

"It's unintended and often indirect but the people hurt the most when aid is cut back are not a country's leaders but those least able to fend for themselves," said a Western aid worker visiting the Seeing Hands clinic for a massage.
Vattana and his colleagues were trained in therapeutic massage by Maryknoll, the American Catholic relief mission.
The project was one of a number that Maryknoll mounted to help disadvantaged Cambodians make themselves self-sufficient.
But the recent turmoil in Phnom Penh has gutted Seeing Hands' business as it has that of hotels, restaurants and travel companies who depend on tourists.

To make matters worse, Washington recently suspended aid to Cambodia for 30 days as a sign of its displeasure at the violent overthrow of First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh by his Second Prime Minister and long-time rival, Hun Sen.
Vattana and his colleagues don't depend on aid, nor on the custom of relief workers.
But they are afraid the United States, possibly followed by other major foreign powers, will send a not-so-subtle signal that Cambodia is an outlaw state, thereby discouraging tourism.
Their worry is practical, not political. Vattana, for instance, has a wife and child to support.
Having survived the genocide of Pol Pol only to go blind from illness while studying architecture, Vattana is not bitter about the past but anxious about his and his family's future.
"First there was Pol Pot and then I went blind and it seemed like half my life was gone," the masseur explained.

"All I had ever wanted to see and know and do was impossible. Then Maryknoll helped me learn this skill and gave me some hope. In normal times I think my life would get better and better. If things don't get back to normal I don't know what I will do."
